sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do the main image and the headline make one idea together, with neither just repeating the other?** The answer is no, because the hero has no main image. The headline and button sit in the left half (x 64–650, y 120–380). The right half (about x 680–1216, y 90–400) is empty white. A viewer gets the promise "Booking links that fill your calendar" but never sees a booking link, a booking page or a filled calendar. The product stays abstract, and the empty half looks like a picture that failed to load rather than space left on purpose. If an image is meant to be there, it is a loading problem and needs checking in a live browser. If not, the hero needs a visual that shows the headline's claim, such as a guest's booking page with open slots or a week view filling up, so the picture proves what the words promise. Defect. The pairing rule's source is off the reading list, so treat it as common sense: a booking tool sells by showing what the guest sees. Weight: major.
2. **Within one screen or image, does each kind of element look the same everywhere it appears?** The answer is no, in three places:
   - In the first card, the "New" badge (x 264–308, y 530–553) is solid blue and pushed to the card's right edge. The "Auto", "Email" and "Beta" badges are grey and sit right after their titles.
   - "Shared calendars" wraps to two lines, so its body text and "Learn more" (y 672) sit lower than in the other three cards (y 642). The row's rhythm breaks in the first card, the one the eye reads first.
   - The primary action has two labels: "Start free" in the nav (x 1107–1216) and "Create your link" in the hero. The viewer has to work out whether these are the same step.

   The cards should follow one program (Gerstner, *Designing Programmes*; Nielsen's consistency and standards heuristic). Keep badges in one position, with a different color only if "New" really should outrank the rest. Make the first title fit on one line (shorter wording, or a badge that drops below the title) so all four cards line up. Give the one primary action one label. Convention. Weight: minor.
3. **Does every element, rule, box, and ornament do a job, so that removing it would lose something?** The answer is no for some of the badges:
   - "Email" on Reminders (x 793–843, y 516–538) reads as a limit ("only email?") more than a feature.
   - "Auto" on Time zones repeats what the body text already says.

   Each badge takes a moment of attention and gives little back. "New" and "Beta" carry real status, so keep those. Drop "Auto", and either drop "Email" or name the channels in the body text. Taste/common sense. The ornament entries cite no approved source. Weight: minor.
4. **Does each heading name what its section holds?** The answer is no for the strip of names at y 770 (Harbor Dental … Orchard Vets). It sits under a hairline rule with no label, in grey text that looks like a footer or a second nav. A viewer may not read these as customers, so the social proof the strip is there for can be missed. Add a short label such as "Used by clinics, tutors and coaches", or show the names as logos. Convention (WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.6, applied loosely to a visible section label). Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- The headline names the outcome rather than the feature, and the subline says exactly what happens: "share one link, let people pick a time… keep every meeting in the right place". A first-time viewer can say what this is for in one sentence.
- Type, color and shapes stay inside one restrained system: one blue, neutral greys, one sans and the same corner radius on buttons, cards and badges. The calm, orderly mood suits a scheduling tool.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Whether the empty right half of the hero is a picture or animation that hadn't loaded when the screenshot was taken. Check it in a live browser.
- What sits below the fold: the customer strip is cut off at the bottom edge.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 4 yes, 4 no (main image and headline make one idea; each kind of element looks the same everywhere; every element does a job; each heading names its section), 0 unsure

**Walk (working notes)**

First read: the eye lands on the headline "Booking links that fill your calendar" (about 48 px, heavy, near-black, top left). It goes down to the blue "Create your link" button, then across the four feature cards. The blue "New" pill on the first card and the blue "Start free" button at top right pull a little, but neither competes with the headline. This reads as a landing page for a scheduling SaaS aimed at small service businesses (the customer row lists dental, tutoring, physio, coaching and vets). It feels clean, calm and standard. Job (assumed): get a small-business owner to understand the product and click "Create your link".

What matters first:
- Does one element clearly dominate? **Yes.** The headline is far larger and heavier than anything else.
- Can each level below it be told from the next at a glance? **Yes.** I count these levels: headline about 48 px bold; subhead about 19 px regular grey; card titles about 20 px bold; body and nav about 15 px; customer names about 14 px grey. The subhead and the card titles are about the same size, but they differ in weight and colour and are never next to each other. The customer names are only about 1 px smaller than body text, but they differ in colour and in role. That is borderline, but they don't get mixed up.
- Where headings are larger, do they also differ in weight, form or colour? **Yes.** Card titles are bold dark text over regular grey-dark body text.

All three lines are yes, so I opened no entries.

---

**Section.** What matters first (hierarchy): applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **One clear place to start.** The headline (about x 64–645, y 120–225) is about 2.5 times the next largest type and the heaviest weight on the page. The eye has one obvious starting point, and from there it drops straight to the single filled blue button below. The path is headline, then subhead, then "Create your link", with no detours.
- **The type levels hold apart without many sizes.** Each of the four cards uses a bold title over regular body text over a bold, underlined "Learn more". Even where the subhead and card titles are nearly the same size (about 19 vs about 20 px), weight and colour keep them on different levels. Contrast comes from weight and colour rather than more sizes (Refactoring UI). Keep this when revising.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

Arrangement walk (working notes). The image is about one screen (1280×800), so I worked from the whole image. Bash isn't allowed in this session, so I couldn't run `crop.mjs` or `entries.mjs`.

- One grid: yes. The four cards sit at x≈64/358/652/946 with about 25 px gutters. The left edge at 64 and the right edge at about 1216 repeat from the nav to the cards to the rule.
- Exact alignment, no near-misses: no. The nav links span about 473–781, so their centre is about 627 px. The page centre and the centre of the card row are both 640 px.
- Baselines across columns: no. In card 1 the title wraps to two lines, so its body and "Learn more" sit about 30 px lower than in cards 2–4.
- Space inside groups smaller than between: yes. The gap above the logo strip is borderline but reads.
- One group per box: yes.
- Only related elements look alike: no. Card 1's badge is pushed to the right edge in solid blue, while the other three badges sit grey right after their titles. The blue badge looks like a different kind of thing and matches the CTAs.
- Nothing overlapping or touching: yes.
- Margins from the edge: yes.
- Empty space gathered: yes. There is one large void, but it is a balance problem (next line).
- Balance: no. The right half of the hero (about x 660–1216, y 100–380) is empty, so the top tips left.
- Centring by reason: yes.
- One proportion: yes. The hero copy fills about the left half.
- Eye path: yes.

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **The visual weight should balance, with no side looking about to tip. It doesn't.** The headline, subhead and CTAs all sit in the left half of the hero (x≈64–645). The right half, about x 660–1216 by y 90–390, is completely empty above a full-width row of cards. The top of the page looks lopsided and unfinished. A product shot, or a booking-page mockup, almost certainly belongs there: hero layouts like this normally have one, and an empty space that size reads as an image that failed to load. That costs credibility in the first second, and the viewer also loses the quickest way to see what a "booking link" looks like.
   - **Fix:** If an image is meant to go there, make sure it renders. If not, put something in the right half that shows the product, such as a sample booking page with time slots. Or rebalance by widening the hero copy or centring the hero over the card row.
   - **Source:** Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, on balance.
   - **Type:** defect, unless the screenshot simply missed an image. **Weight:** major.
2. **Lines of text in neighbouring columns should sit on the same baselines. They don't.** In card 1, "Shared calendars" wraps to two lines (y≈527 and 557) because the "New" badge takes space at the right edge. Its body starts at about y 590 and "Learn more" sits at about y 672. In cards 2–4 the body starts at about y 560 and "Learn more" sits at about y 642. The row of four looks ragged, and the first card looks broken.
   - **Fix:** Let card 1's badge sit right after the title, as it does in the other cards, so the title stays on one line. Or align body text and links across the row whatever the title length.
   - **Type:** convention (Bringhurst, cross-column alignment), and the visible cost is real. **Weight:** minor.
3. **Only related elements should look alike. Here the badges don't match each other, and one matches the buttons instead.** Card 1's "New" badge (about x 264–308, y 541) is solid blue and pushed to the card's right edge. "Auto", "Email" and "Beta" are pale grey and sit right after their titles. The four badges don't read as one set. The blue pill also has the same blue as "Start free" and "Create your link", so it looks clickable.
   - **Fix:** Give all four badges the same placement. Keep the blue for things you can click.
   - **Type:** defect (mixed signals), partly taste. **Weight:** minor.
4. **Every element should be exactly aligned with an axis it shares with another, or clearly off it. The nav links are a near-miss.** The links span about x 473–781, so their centre is about 627 px. The page centre and the centre of the card row are both 640 px. A 13 px offset reads as a mistake, not a choice. This is by eye; measure the nav group's box against the viewport centre.
   - **Fix:** Centre the links exactly on the page, or line them up with a column edge on purpose.
   - **Type:** convention (common sense, alignment). **Weight:** minor.

**What's working.** The four cards use a strict grid: equal widths, gutters of about 25 px, and outer edges that match the 64 px margins of the logo, the hero copy and the rule. That is what makes the row read as one set. The vertical spacing also steps up in a sensible order: headline to subhead to CTAs are close together, and the gap down to the cards is larger. So the hero reads as one unit before the features.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether the empty right half of the hero is a missing or lazy-loaded image. Check it in a live browser. How the four cards reflow at narrower widths, where the wrapped-title mismatch in card 1 will probably get worse.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 9 yes, 4 no (exact alignment with no near-misses; baselines across columns; only related elements look alike; visual weight balances), 0 unsure.

sections.report:
**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do headings and captions break at phrase boundaries, never between a number and its unit or inside a name?** There are two breaks, both of the same kind.
   - **Hero headline (about x 64–645, y 120–225).** It reads "Booking links that fill your / calendar". The break splits "your" from "calendar", so the second line is a single word. The headline reads as a sentence that stalls, and the payoff word sits alone under a wide empty area. There is about 570 px of empty space to the right of the headline (x 645–1216), so the wrap comes from a narrow text box, not from a lack of room. Fix: widen the headline box so it sets on one line, or break it at a phrase, such as "Booking links / that fill your calendar".
   - **First card heading (x 90–190, y 515–570).** "Shared / calendars" breaks inside the feature's name because the "New" badge takes up the width. The other three card titles sit on one line. Card 1's title is therefore two lines, which pushes its body text and "Learn more" link about 30 px below the other cards (y 672 against y 642). That breaks the row across all four cards. Fix: keep the name on one line by shortening it (for example "Team calendars"), or move the badge above or below the title.

   This is taste/common sense. The catalog entry's source for heading breaks is marked unverified, so no published rule backs it. Weight: minor. The page still works, but these are the two most visible text flaws.

**What's working.**
- **Type scale and family.** The page uses one sans family with a short, clear scale: headline about 48 px bold, subhead about 19 px, card titles about 20 px semibold, body about 15 px, labels about 12–14 px. Each size has an obvious job, and weight separates the levels rather than near-identical sizes.
- **Subhead length.** The subhead runs about 65 characters a line over two lines, with comfortable line spacing. Lines that length read in one pass.

**Checklist.** `Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (headings break at phrase boundaries)`

sections.report:
**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **One accent colour, used only for actions.** The page uses one neutral range (white, light grey card borders, mid-grey icons and pills, near-black text) and a single saturated blue. That blue appears in only three places: "Start free" (about 1107–1216, 10–52), "Create your link" (about 64–247, 325–377) and the small "New" pill on the first card. Because so little of the page is coloured, the eye goes straight to the two buttons and the next step is clear. The headline handles hierarchy in black and white, so the colour doesn't have to. This is the accent restraint that Wathan and Schoger's *Refactoring UI* argues for. Keep the blue to actions and to at most one marker. The "New" pill already borrows the action blue, so a second coloured badge would start to blur what blue means on this page.
- **The structure still shows in greyscale.** Black headline, grey body text, grey icons and pale card borders give enough steps of light and dark that the layout holds together without its one hue. The blue buttons also read as the darkest solid blocks on the page. Every meaning has a non-colour cue too: the badges are text ("New", "Auto", "Email", "Beta") and the links are underlined, so nothing depends on colour alone.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Pictures applies. The only pictures are the four small feature-card icons and the "Slotwise" wordmark. There are no photos or illustrations, and the customer names are plain text.

**Findings**
1. **Do the icons and line drawings share one stroke weight, cap style, and corner radius? No.** The calendar icon in the first card (about x 94–122, y 460–488) is drawn as a thin outline with a solid header bar. The other three are solid filled shapes: the clock (about x 386–418) is a solid disc with the hands cut out, the envelope (about x 682–710) is solid, and the layout glyph (about x 976–1002) is solid blocks. Next to the three solid shapes, the calendar looks lighter and reads as if it came from another icon set. The row looks assembled rather than drawn as one family, and the first card, which also has the "New" badge, looks slightly unfinished. Apple's Human Interface Guidelines ("Icons") say that a set of interface icons should use a consistent level of detail and stroke thickness (or weight). The fix is to draw all four in one style from one family: either all solid, by swapping in the filled calendar, or all outline at one stroke weight. Convention. Weight: minor, because the icons only decorate the cards and the headings carry the meaning.

**What's working.** The icons stay quiet and support the text. They are small, a single mid-grey, and all the same size, so they mark each card without pulling attention from the "Create your link" button or the card headings. The "Slotwise" wordmark is a plain bold wordmark with plenty of space around it, so it stays readable at any size and in one colour.

**Checklist.** Pictures: 12 lines, 11 yes, 1 no (icons share one stroke weight, cap style and corner radius)

sections.report:
**Section.** Interface: applies. The page has navigation, two filled buttons, text links and cards. The image is 1280×800, about one screen, so I worked from the whole image. Bash was denied, so I could not run the crop and entries scripts. The findings below rest on the checklist lines and the canon, not on the full catalog entries.

**Findings**
1. **"Is exactly one button styled as the primary action, with every other action styled lower?"** The header button "Start free" (about x 1107–1215, y 10–52) and the hero button "Create your link" (about x 64–246, y 325–377) are the same filled blue at about the same weight, but their labels differ. A first-time viewer sees two equal calls to action with different promises: one about a free plan, one about making a link. They can't tell whether these do the same thing or which one to press. Repeating the call to action in the header is a common convention and costs nothing on its own. The cost comes from the two names. Fix: give both the same label, or keep the hero as the one strong button and step the header button down a level, for example an outline button. Convention (Refactoring UI; Nielsen Norman Group on primary vs. secondary actions). Minor.
2. **"Does every control look like what it does, buttons pressable, fields typeable, and links marked by more than color?"** The "New" badge on the Shared calendars card (about x 264–308, y 530–553) is a solid pill in the same blue as both buttons. It looks like a tiny button, and the viewer may try to click it. It also pulls more attention than its own card heading. The other badges ("Auto", "Email", "Beta") are pale grey and read as tags, so this one blue badge is out of step with them. Fix: keep that blue for things you can click, and make "New" a tag like the others, set apart by a tint or outline rather than the action colour. Convention (Norman, signifiers). Minor.
3. **"Do the navigation and components follow the conventions users know from the platform and similar products?"** The header has no "Log in" or "Sign in" link. Most SaaS sites put one next to the main header button, so returning customers look there. Here they would have to guess, perhaps that "Start free" also handles sign-in, or go searching. Fix: add a quiet "Log in" text link just left of "Start free". Convention (Jakob's law, Nielsen Norman Group). Minor, because this page is mainly for new visitors, but it is a daily cost for existing customers.
4. **"Can each link's purpose be told from its text or the sentence around it?"** All four cards end with the same link text, "Learn more" (about y 642 and y 672). On screen, the card heading gives each link its meaning. But anyone moving through links one at a time, such as a screen-reader user, hears "Learn more" four times with nothing to tell them apart. This counts as a `no` unless each link is tied to its card heading in the code. Fix: name the subject in the link ("More on time zones") or tie the link to the heading in the code. Convention (WCAG 2.4.4). Minor.
5. **"Do labels and messages use the audience's own words rather than internal or system terms?"** The badges "Auto" (time zones) and "Email" (reminders) are terse tags in the same pill shape as the status badges "New" and "Beta", so the viewer can't tell what kind of thing a badge says. "Email" could mean the feature only sends email, or that email is one option. "Auto" could mean automatic detection or a setting. Fix: drop these two badges, or say it in the card text ("detected automatically", "by email or SMS"), and keep badges for status only. Taste / common sense. Minor.

**What's working.**
- "See a live example" is set clearly below "Create your link": it is an underlined bold text link next to the filled button. The viewer gets one obvious action and a low-commitment second one, and the second also lets them see the value for themselves before signing up.
- The text links are underlined and bold, not marked by colour alone. The nav is in the usual places: logo left, sections centre, call to action right. Nothing in it needs learning.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Hover, focus and pressed states for the buttons, nav links and "Learn more" links (including whether focus is visible). Whether the whole of each card is clickable or only its link. Whether the header is sticky, and whether it would then cover focused controls as the page scrolls.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 25 yes, 5 no (one primary action; controls look like what they do; platform conventions; link purpose; audience's own words), 3 unsure (states shown distinct; focus indicator; focus not obscured)
